items.text: Trump-Xi summit takes shape as a de facto AI summit: two-day Washington visit begins Sept. 23, state dinner Sept. 24 with Altman, Huang and Cook on the guest list.
Four subscribers filed a federal class action against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI alleging Amodei's 'slow down' essay masked an illegal coordination pact.
Nscale filed to go public on the NYSE (ticker NSCL), reporting a $1.02B net loss on 1,252% revenue growth, backed by Nvidia and Microsoft.
Chip stocks and bitcoin rallied Monday ahead of the Xi summit; Nasdaq led gains as oil prices fell.
Alibaba open-sourced Qwen-Image-2.1, a 7B image model, but switched to a research-only license requiring paid grants for commercial use.
Google's AX (Agent Executor), an Apache-2.0 agent orchestrator built on Agent Substrate, hit v0.3.0 and topped Hacker News.
Tencent-backed Naive AI hit a $1.42B valuation on $400M raised, seven months after founding and before shipping a model.
Ayar Labs added $150M, pushing its 2026 optical-interconnect fundraising total to $650M.
Blackstone secured a UBS term loan to help fund its acquisition of data-center cooling maker Flow Control Holdings from Audax.

categories.subhead: A press-freedom lawsuit and an AI safety pact both come due the same day the Trump-Xi summit clock starts ticking

stories.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue Trump administration over White House press ban
body: CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed suit Monday after the White House revoked their journalists' hard-pass credentials over the weekend, with the outlets saying in a joint statement that the government had acted "without notice or process" because it "objected to our reporting."

Secret Service agents seized the badges of MS NOW's Akayla Gardner, CNN's Betsy Klein and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett on Saturday as they tried to enter the White House grounds, two days after Trump said he was barring the outlets over what he called years of unfair, negative coverage.

The case was assigned to Judge Timothy Kelly — a Trump appointee who in 2018 ordered the first Trump White House to restore CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's credentials — and the outlets have already filed a motion for a temporary restraining order to force immediate reinstatement of access.

First Amendment attorney Ted Boutrous, who represented CNN in the 2018 Acosta case, is leading the new suit and called the ban "a direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process."
stories.callback: Yesterday: Bloomberg's AI newsletter flagged the press-access fight as a subplot to the Trump-Xi run-up. Today: it became a full First Amendment lawsuit, filed the same morning AI policy dominates the news cycle.

stories.headline: Bessent and Chinese counterpart open AI, tariff and rare-earth talks in New York ahead of Trump-Xi summit
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met for hours with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday, with the U.S. proposing a new AI safety notification mechanism as part of the broader trade and technology talks setting the stage for this week's summit.

Chinese state media acknowledged only that the two sides "discussed AI," a notably thinner readout than the American side's framing, underscoring the gap between Washington's push for coordinated AI safeguards and Beijing's reluctance to formally commit to one.

Separately, the United Nations' Independent AI Panel issued its first thematic brief on Monday urging governments to rein in autonomous AI agents, adding international pressure just as U.S. and Chinese officials debate what, if any, joint safety architecture the two countries might accept.

Xi is set to land at Joint Base Andrews on September 23 with a state dinner the following night; Trump and Xi's only prior 2026 meeting, in Beijing in May, produced no formal agreements on AI or chip export controls.
stories.callback: Yesterday: we covered the summit's guest list and modest expectations for a breakthrough. Today: Bessent and He Lifeng actually sat down in New York, with the U.S. floating a concrete AI safety notification mechanism.

stories.headline: Anthropic makes Accenture its first 'embedded evaluator,' the first concrete piece of Amodei's slowdown plan
body: Anthropic and Accenture announced Friday that Accenture staff — via its Faculty AI unit — will be embedded inside Anthropic with employee-level access to red-team models, run alignment assessments and test safeguards, with each company expecting to invest at least $1 billion over five years.

The move operationalizes the first phase of CEO Dario Amodei's three-step plan to "pace the frontier," unveiled September 12, which called for independent safety evaluators and industry coordination rather than unilateral deceleration.

Anthropic said the arrangement does not reduce its own accountability for model safety and that it is in separate talks with the nonprofit METR and other evaluators, since "there are, as yet, no standards for what information embedded evaluators should have access to."

The announcement lands squarely inside the fight over Amodei's proposal: a federal class action filed last week accuses Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI of using that same slowdown pact to illegally coordinate and shortchange paying subscribers.
stories.callback: Yesterday: we covered the class-action lawsuit accusing the labs of colluding under cover of Amodei's slowdown essay. Today: Anthropic put a dollar figure and a named partner behind the first plank of that same plan.

categories.subhead: The AI trade roars back to life on Wall Street as chipmakers reprice for a summit and an inference boom

stories.headline: AMD tops $1 trillion market cap as chip stocks lead a broad Monday rally
body: Chipmaker AMD soared to an all-time high above $610 a share, giving it a $1 trillion market cap during Monday's trading session, while Arm Holdings and Intel both jumped roughly 10%.

The Nasdaq Composite surged as oil prices retreated and Treasury yields fell, with strategists pointing to "a persistent growth/AI risk-on bias" across Nvidia, Amazon, Alphabet and bitcoin heading into the Trump-Xi summit later this week.

Asian markets echoed the move overnight, with technology and semiconductor stocks leading gains, while the rally follows a volatile prior week in which the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years and the Dow logged its worst weekly performance since March.
stories.callback: Yesterday: we noted chip stocks and bitcoin rallying ahead of the summit dinner. Today: the rally accelerated further, pushing AMD past a $1 trillion valuation.

stories.headline: AMD reportedly plans to raise prices on AI accelerators and GPUs by around 10%
body: AMD shares jumped over 9% Monday following reports that the chipmaker plans to raise prices by roughly 10% on some AI accelerators and GPUs, a move that lands as the company's market cap crosses the $1 trillion threshold.

The reported price increase comes amid persistent supply constraints across the AI hardware market, where demand for training and inference silicon continues to outstrip capacity even as rivals like Nvidia and Qualcomm expand their own data-center chip lines.

categories.subhead: Yesterday's coding-tool crown gets an asterisk as a fresh benchmark shows the race is basically tied
Hollywood's biggest pending merger clears its last major legal hurdle

stories.headline: Paramount settles state antitrust suits, clearing the path for its $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger
body: Paramount Skydance reached a settlement with California and the coalition of state attorneys general suing to block its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, according to people familiar with the matter, with the deal expected to be formally announced Monday.

The settlement came together over the weekend after several holdout states — including New York and Connecticut, which had been pushing for stronger job-protection guarantees and firmer editorial independence commitments for CNN and CBS News — dropped their objections to terms California AG Rob Bonta had negotiated.

Paramount CEO David Ellison thanked Bonta, the WGA and California Governor Newsom "for engaging in good faith to find a path forward," while Bonta stressed at a Los Angeles press conference that the settlement was not an endorsement of the underlying deal.

The merger, first agreed in February at $31 a share and $110 billion including debt, still faces a separate Writers Guild of America antitrust suit, but the state settlement removes the biggest remaining obstacle — and stops the clock on a $7-million-a-day fee Paramount owes Warner Bros. shareholders starting October 1 until the deal closes.
